1. Introduction
Previous tra(cid:129)c noise prediction model studies have indicated that sound absorp-
tive materials can reduce noise levels substantially especially where barriers are
placed on both sides of the road and there is a possibility of multiple reflections

been reported from such studies [1–3]. However some studies at the roadside have
reported no significant increase in noise when a single reflective barrier was erected
on the far side [4,5]. There was therefore a need to further investigate the acoustics
benefitsoftypicalroadsidebarriersinordertofullyvalidateand,ifnecessary,refine
predictionmodels.
2. Method
The method involved the measurement of roadside A-weighted noise levels where
amodularnoiseabsorptivebarrierhadbeenconstructed.Measurementsweretaken
with thebarrier panels in thenormal position, i.e. with theabsorptive face opposite
the tra(cid:129)c and then measurements were repeated with the panels reversed such that
the reflective face was facing the tra(cid:129)c. It was possible to identify only two sites
where barriers which contained absorptive panels which could be readily reversed.
At both sites the same absorptive panels had been employed. The panels were rela-
tively light consisting of an aluminium box with mineral fibre fill and they were
secured by I-section steel posts which greatly assisted with the reversal operation.
Thetra(cid:129)csideofthepanelswereperforatedwhichallowedthepenetrationofsound
waves and the absorption of sound energy in the fibrous fill material. The reverse
sidewasplaneandwithoutperforationsandwassoundreflective.Trialsatthenoise
barriertest facility (NBTF)at TRL demonstrated the highly reflectivenature of the
reverse side [3]. The bottom 0.5 m of the barrier consisted of a concrete ground
beam.
The absorptive face of the panels had very good acoustic performance from 250
Hzto5kHzwitharandomincidenceabsorptioncoe(cid:129)cientofapproximately0.9at
frequenciescloseto1kHzwhichisatthepeakintheA-weightedspectrumoftypical
highway tra(cid:129)c noise. Fig. 1 shows the variation of sound absorption in one-third
octavebandsfrom100to5kHz.TrialsattheNBTFconfirmed thatthisperforated
face was veryabsorptive [3].
The noise logging equipment employed at the two sites consisted of a computer
based sound level meter which allowed simultaneous measurements of L , L ,

latter was placed some distance away so that it would not be influenced by changes

levels inaprevious study wasadopted[6].Someprevious studieshave attemptedto

where 3 m barriers were erected on the farside the noise levels behind the nearside
barrier varied from an increase of 0.7 dB(A) to a decrease of 1.6 dB(A) with the
average level decreasing by 0.2 dB(A). In a study where noise reflections from a

3. Analysis
For both before and after measurements at the two sites the di(cid:128)erences in A-
weighted sound pressure levels between the measurement and reference positions
were computed for each ten minute period. In this way any variation of source
strength due to such factors as tra(cid:129)c flow, speed and composition was controlled.
Thesedi(cid:128)erenceswereregressedagainsttheaveragecomponentsofwindspeedboth
normal and parallel to the barrier. To normalize the data for zero wind speed, the
average components of wind speed were calculated for each 10-min recording per-
iod. This method has been developed for previous studies [3,6]. Multiple regression
was carried out and analysis of variance was used to obtain the predicted level dif-
ferences at zero wind speed (i.e. where both normal and parallel components were
zero) and the standard error of the mean di(cid:128)erence. Changes in the noise level dif-
ferencesfollowingthealterationstothebarrierweretestedforstatisticalsignificance
by adding the variances of the mean di(cid:128)erences and using the Student t values to
determine the 95% confidence limits. Where the confidence band included zero the
change was not statistically significant atthe 5% level.

The measured changes in tra(cid:129)c noise caused by replacing an absorptive material
by reflective material on roadside barriers were generally smaller than the appro-
priate corrections for reflective barriers provided in the UK tra(cid:129)c noise prediction
model CRTN. As a consequence, omitting the reflection correction in CRTN, in
order to predict reductions in noise levels due to the inclusion of highly absorptive
materials in barriers, may lead to an over-estimate of the acoustic benefits particu-
larly atreceivers close to theroad.
Predictive models have tended to overestimate the e(cid:128)ect of absorptive barriers.
The analysis in the present study has indicated that scattering by the vehicle stream
and associated turbulence, and the simplified geometries and acoustic performances
of barrier panels assumed in such models can contribute to these discrepancies.
